summary: Describes the operating model of Cabletron's SecureFast VLAN product, which uses virtual LANs to decide whether connection requests are allowed and to limit broadcasts. It is a vendor description published as informational.

eli5.summary: One physical set of cables is split into private groups, and a connection is allowed only when both sides belong to the same group.

questions: how do vlans control network traffic
how does connection oriented switching work
subtitle: A distributed connection-oriented switching system that uses virtual LANs to control traffic between endpoints.

tldr.problem: Switches need a way to enforce network policies that control which devices can communicate, limit broadcast flooding to specific groups, and route traffic through the network fabric efficiently based on business rules rather than just destination addresses.
tldr.mechanism: Cabletron's SecureFast VLAN (SFVLAN) uses virtual LANs (logical groups of ports) to segment the network. When a packet arrives, the switch establishes a call connection (a state entry) that maps the source and destination address pair to specific ports. Policies determine whether each connection is allowed based on VLAN membership. The system uses centralized directory services, spanning tree for flooding, and link state protocols for finding optimal paths.
tldr.outcome: Networks can restrict traffic between different groups (VLANs), intercept and resolve broadcasts at the ingress, limit broadcast flooding to same-VLAN ports, and automatically reroute connections when links fail. This provided fine-grained traffic control and broadcast containment on switched networks.

today: RFC 2643 is an Informational document describing Cabletron's proprietary SFVLAN switching architecture. The protocol is now primarily of historical interest, though it pioneered connection-oriented switching and VLAN-based traffic control on Cabletron switches. Modern Ethernet switching has largely adopted simpler bridge-based VLAN approaches.

sections.title: Introduction to SFVLAN
sections.content:
RFC 2643 describes Cabletron's SecureFast VLAN (SFVLAN) product, a distributed connection-oriented switching protocol that runs at the MAC layer. Unlike traditional bridge-based networks, SFVLAN establishes explicit call connections for each source-destination address pair, allowing switches to enforce policies and control traffic flow.

The RFC documents the operational model of SFVLAN, including how virtual LANs (VLANs) segment the network, how call connections are established and routed, and how the system maintains consistency across multiple switches. SFVLAN uses four major service centers to handle directory service, topology, route resolution, and policy enforcement.

This is a vendor-specific implementation published as Informational to document the protocol design, not a standard for interoperability.
sections.eli5: This is a system where switches create and track individual connections for traffic between specific computers, and use VLAN membership to decide whether to allow each connection.

sections.title: VLAN Principles and Configuration
sections.content:
A Virtual LAN (VLAN) is a logical grouping of ports and endstations. All ports and endstations in a VLAN behave as if they are on the same physical network segment, even if they are geographically separated across the switch fabric.

Each switch port is assigned a default VLAN. At startup, all ports belong to a base VLAN. When an endstation attaches to a port, it initially inherits the port's default VLAN, but can be reassigned to another VLAN by a network administrator using the VLAN Manager application.

There are two configuration modes for endstations: inherited (belongs to its port's default VLAN) and static (belongs to a VLAN assigned by the administrator). For ports, there are two modes: normal (inherited endstations follow the port's VLAN; static endstations keep their assigned VLAN) and locked (all endstations must belong to the port's default VLAN).

Each VLAN has a policy value: either Open (allows connections between endstations in the VLAN) or Secure (enforces connection validation before allowing traffic). VLAN membership determines both whether a call connection is allowed and which ports receive flooded (broadcast) messages.
sections.eli5: Each port gets assigned to a VLAN group. Computers plugged into that port join the same group. When a computer wants to send to another, the switches check if they are in the same group before allowing the connection.

sections.title: Connection-Oriented Switching Architecture
sections.content:
SFVLAN is connection-oriented: when a packet with a source/destination address pair arrives, the switch establishes a call connection -- an entry that maps that address pair and incoming port to a specific outgoing port. Once the connection is established, all future packets with that address pair arriving on that port are automatically forwarded to the same outport by the switch hardware, without requiring a new lookup.

A distributed switching environment requires each switch to coordinate. SFVLAN accomplishes this through four service centers:

Directory Service Center: Maintains a virtual directory of all endstations and their locations across the fabric. The Local Add Server registers new endstations as they attach; the Inverse Resolve Server finds endstations by address; the Local Delete Server removes endstations when they disconnect.

Topology Service Center: Discovers neighbors and maintains a loop-free flood path using spanning tree. The Neighbor Discovery Server detects which switches are adjacent; the Spanning Tree Server calculates a loop-free tree; the Link State Server maintains topology information.

Resolve Service Center: Converts destination addresses to switch locations. Servers handle table lookups, local ports, subnets, and unresolvable addresses.

Policy Service Center: Enforces VLAN policies. The Unicast Rules Server determines whether a call connection request should be allowed based on VLAN membership.

Two additional service centers handle routing (Path Service Center, using link state information) and broadcast scoping (Flood Service Center, restricting broadcasts to same-VLAN ports).
sections.eli5: The system has several helpers: one keeps track of where computers are, one figures out how data flows through the switches, one looks up addresses, one enforces the VLAN rules, and one makes sure broadcasts only reach the right group.

sections.title: Call Processing and Routing
sections.content:
When a packet arrives at an ingress switch (the switch where the source is attached), the switch must determine the path to the egress switch (where the destination is attached) and establish a call connection.

A call connection path is a set of 0 to 7 network links (switch-to-switch connections) over which traffic travels. Paths are selected from a list of equal-cost paths calculated by the VLSP protocol. The switch chooses among these to load balance traffic.

The path from ingress to egress can have zero links (both endstations on the same switch), one link (neighbor switches), or multiple links through intermediate switches. Intermediate switches forward packets along established connections without re-evaluating the destination address.

SFVLAN automatically reroutes connections when links fail or switches become unavailable, using alternate equal-cost paths provided by the link state protocol.

Broadcast packets are handled specially: broadcasts are intercepted at the ingress port, the destination address is resolved, and the switch floods the packet only to ports belonging to the same VLAN as the source, reducing unnecessary broadcast traffic across the fabric.
sections.eli5: When a computer sends data to another, the ingress switch finds the best path, sets up the connection, and tells intermediate switches to forward the traffic. If a link breaks, it automatically uses a backup path.

sections.title: Interswitch Communication
sections.content:
Switches communicate through the InterSwitch Message Protocol (ISMP), which SFVLAN uses to coordinate topology information, resolve addresses, and manage connections.

ISMP message types include:

BPDU Messages and Remote Blocking Messages: Used for spanning tree calculation, determining a loop-free path for flooding undirected messages to all switches.

Resolve Messages: Used to query other switches for the location of an endstation address. Responses provide the switch ID where the endstation is attached.

New User Messages: Notify other switches when an endstation attaches or detaches, maintaining directory consistency.

Tag-Based Flood Messages: Broadcast messages that respect VLAN boundaries. Switches forward these only to ports in the originating VLAN.

Tap/Untap Messages: Used for monitoring (tapping) traffic between two endstations, useful for debugging and troubleshooting.

Each ISMP packet includes a frame header (MAC layer), an ISMP packet header (version, message type, originator), and a message body with specific content for each message type.
sections.eli5: Switches send each other messages to share which computers are where, maintain the loop-free tree, find destinations, and decide where to send broadcasts.
